This Range Rover Sport Costs Less Than a New Base Toyota Corolla, Would You Buy It?
21 photos
Photo: Instagram | automotive_ambitions
Yeah, it is not exactly an all-new Range Rover Sport , as you can clearly see from the pictures shared below, as what we are looking at here is the previous generation, more particularly, an example that is looking for a new home in the States as we speak, with a used car dealer behind the ad.
Before we get into the details, we have to admit that the second generation has aged very nicely, and to be honest, the first one is not that bad either. The latter was made between 2006 and 2013, sharing its nuts and bolts with the Land Rover Discovery (L319), and the former builds on the same bones as the L462 Discovery, as well as the era’s Range Rover, aka its bigger and more expensive sibling.
Production took place at the Solihull facility in the United Kingdom between 2013 and 2022. The second-gen Range Rover Sport was offered with numerous gasoline engines, including a mild-hybrid, a plug-in hybrid, and even a V8, and it also came with diesel power on the right side of the Atlantic Ocean. All versions featured the same ZF-made eight-speed automatic transmission, and this model was 191 inches (4,851 mm) long, 81.6 inches (2,073 mm) wide with the mirrors folded, 71.3 inches (1,811 mm) tall, and had 115.1 inches (2,924 mm) between the axles.
It was designed by Gerry McGovern, who also left his mark on other Land Rovers, including the Range Rover, the Discovery 4, Discovery Sport, and new Defender, among others. The second-gen Range Rover Sport celebrated its public debut back in 2013 at the New York Auto Show (ah, the good old days when auto shows were still big!), and four years later, it was facelifted and unveiled at the 2017 Los Angeles Auto Show.
Photo: Instagram | automotive_ambitions Given that it has aged like fine wine rather than fine milk, and that it still looks very modern both inside and out, one might assume that they need to be loaded if they dream about owning such a thing. But that’s not the case, because this model can sell for as little as $10,000 in today’s used car market in the United States of America. That’s for base grades that have seen plenty of action over the years, and are not exactly in top-notch condition anymore.
Mid-spec variants from mid-model years fetch from $13,000 to roughly $35,000, and they can also go for over $45,000 for low-mileage examples in good overall shape. Later model years tend to go between $19,000 and over $50,000, and it is these that you may want to get, because they usually still have a lot of life left in them, as long as you go for a nicely maintained one with plenty of service history.
As for the pictured machine, it is a 2019 model year Range Rover Sport in the HSE configuration. The images reveal that it sports a dark overall look on the outside. It is finished in Narvic Black, the vendor reveals, has a body-colored roof, rides on a set of multi-spoke alloys with the OEM center caps, and sports red brake calipers, which are the only things providing some contrast to the SUV’s darkened overall appearance.
Photo: Instagram | automotive_ambitions The interior is also black, and it features black leather upholstery on the seats and on other touchable components. The headliner is also presented in black, and some of the onboard gear includes the sliding panoramic roof, a heated windscreen, a heated steering wheel, Interior Protection & Storage Pack, blind spot monitoring, and others that haven’t been mentioned in the ad on social media that we will link toward the end of this story.
For whatever reason, the vendor chose not to mention the oily bits at all, so we cannot tell you exactly what powers this model . We do know that it came with various powertrain options, depending on the market, including a plug-in hybrid assembly, a supercharged V6 gasoline burner, a supercharged V8, and a pair of diesels that were available on various regional lineups.
What we can tell you instead is that the pictured Range Rover Sport has a clean title, has never been involved in an accident, and has no mileage discrepancies. Speaking of the latter part, it has seen a lot of action over the years, as at the time of cataloging, the odometer read around 92,000 miles (~148,000 km).
Now that you know how much this model usually goes for, and what some of the highlights of the pictured example are, how much do you thing this ride is worth? Not that much compared to what it initially cost, obviously, and at the time of writing, it was advertised for $23,991. That’s actually less than what you’d have to pay for a new base 2027 Toyota Corolla, which has an MSRP of $23,325 in the States for the latest model year. A California trucking company owner pleaded guilty to a $2.1 million fraud scheme involving nearly 100 stolen identities. Hasan Korkmaz, 45, of Las Vegas, operated San Diego Logistics Group Inc. in Santee, California. Federal prosecutors detailed how he processed fraudulent credit card transactions through several businesses, including his trucking operation. Individual charges reached $18,500, ultimately causing more than $2,103,000 in losses across two banks.
Korkmaz admitted to all 18 counts involving bank fraud, money laundering and aggravated identity theft on October 15. The operation ran during 2022 and 2023, using personal information belonging to real individuals. Prosecutors traced proceeds into financial accounts he controlled in Turkey. Korkmaz remained overseas for approximately 18 months before returning to the United States, where authorities arrested him in June 2025.
How the credit card scheme worked
Korkmaz obtained names, birth dates, Social Security numbers and other identifying information to open numerous fraudulent credit card accounts. Prosecutors described the operation as a credit card “bust-out” scheme. The method involves establishing accounts under stolen identities and exhausting available credit without intending to repay the balances. He also submitted checks from nonexistent accounts or those lacking sufficient funds, temporarily restoring credit limits for additional purchases.
San Diego Logistics Group was among the businesses that processed the fraudulent credit card charges. Some individual transactions reached $18,500. Prosecutors did not identify the services associated with those payments. Court filings cited in the DOJ announcement do not establish whether the transactions involved actual freight shipments.
Federal records reveal trucking company’s operating history
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration records identify San Diego Logistics Group Inc. under USDOT 3210732 and MC 1002578. The company reported three trucks, five CDL drivers and 2,948,000 miles traveled in 2022. Its registered cargo categories included general freight, refrigerated food, fresh produce, meat and U.S. mail. The figures came from the carrier’s November 2023 MCS-150 filing.
Divided among three trucks, the reported mileage equals approximately 983,000 miles per truck in one year. The American Transportation Research Institute reported an industry average of 78,863 miles per truck in 2022 . That makes San Diego Logistics Group’s reported mileage more than 12 times the industry average. An inaccurate mileage filing or a larger fleet operating during 2022 could explain the discrepancy.
Neither explanation has been confirmed, and the mileage figures come from the carrier’s own filings. Its registered cargo categories also do not independently establish completed freight deliveries. For brokers, discrepancies like this highlight why carrier verification must go beyond checking operating authority. Federal records do not establish whether the mileage discrepancy had any connection to Korkmaz’s criminal conduct.
FMCSA granted the company’s common carrier authority on December 6, 2021. The agency initiated six involuntary revocation proceedings during 2022 and 2023, subsequently discontinuing each one. FMCSA commonly starts these proceedings when required insurance coverage lapses and may discontinue them after carriers restore compliance. Available records do not establish what triggered each action against San Diego Logistics Group.
Regulators ultimately revoked the company’s common carrier authority on January 2, 2024. Its current registration profile lists both common and broker authority as inactive. Insurance records show previous cancellations and no active primary liability coverage. Federal filings do not establish any connection between those regulatory issues and Korkmaz’s criminal conduct.
Sentencing scheduled for January
The indictment included 12 bank fraud counts, two money laundering charges and four aggravated identity theft offenses. Bank fraud carries a maximum sentence of 30 years per count. Money laundering carries up to 10 years per count under 18 U.S.C. Section 1957. Aggravated identity theft requires a mandatory consecutive two-year prison term. These statutory penalties do not establish the sentence Korkmaz will ultimately receive.
U.S. District Judge James E. Simmons Jr. scheduled sentencing for January 8, 2027, at 9 a.m. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kevin Mokhtari and Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Katherine Rookard are prosecuting case 25-cr-1405-JES. The Justice Department has not identified the banks or explained how Korkmaz obtained the victims’ information.
Why It Matters
A registered trucking company became part of a financial fraud operation that caused more than $2.1 million in losses. The case highlights the importance of examining company ownership, operating authority and financial activity when evaluating transportation businesses.

Rare 1977 Pontiac Can Am Emerges After 30 Years in a Barn, It's an Unrestored Survivor
14 photos
Photo: Craiglist
The Malaise Era was in full swing in 1977. Muscle cars had been stripped off their potent V8 engines in the early years of that decade, and some nameplates had been discontinued for good. The Pontiac GTO , the vehicle credited for having popularized the muscle car, was one of those cars.
With the second-gen model gone after the 1972 model year, the GTO returned as a heavily restyled mid-size car with the "Colonnade" body style. But Pontiac sold only 4,806 units and decided to slap the GTO badge on a compact Ventura in 1974. The latter was a tad more successful with 7,058 examples sold, but Pontiac opted to send the nameplate into the history books.
The company revisited the three years later. It did not revive the GTO but debuted a new performance-oriented model that was also based on the Le Mans. It was called the Can Am, after the then-famous Can-Am racing series, thus continuing the race theme that Pontiac used for the Trans Am and Grand Prix.
The Can Am was the brainchild of Jim Wangers, the man behind the more iconic GTO. Designed to revive the spirit of the original muscle car, the Can Am was based on the LeMans Sport Coupe but used the shaker hood scoop of the Trans Am, while its ducktail spoiler was based on the Grand Am All-American concept car.
Cameo White was the only available exterior color, but the Can Am also got a unique livery with tri-tone stripes in orange, yellow, and gold. More importantly, it was fitted with the W72 400-cubic-inch (6.6-liter) V8 engine from the Trans Am. The mill delivered 200 horsepower, 20 more than the similar unit offered in the LeMans Sport Coupe.
Although 200 horsepower wasn't much compared to the golden-era GTO, it was a pretty solid figure in 1977. Only the Chevrolet Corvette delivered more oomph (210 horsepower), with most of the Can Am's competitors coming with far less on tap. Some cars sold in California were also equipped with a 403-cubic-inch Oldsmobile V8 rated at 185 horsepower.
Pontiac envisioned the Can Am as a limited-edition vehicle, but production was cut shorter than expected when the mold used to produce the fiberglass rear spoiler broke. Because the LeMans was scheduled to be downsized for 1978, Pontiac opted to discontinue the Can Am altogether. Only 1,377 examples were produced.
It's unclear how many of these cars have survived, but I've seen a few pop up for sale in recent years. Some have been restored, while others became rust buckets due to improper storage. The Can Am you see here is somewhere in between. It spent about three decades off the road, but it's not too far gone. Moreover, it's an unaltered survivor.
Hailing from Olathe, Kansas, the Can Am was parked in a barn in 1995 with 106,000 miles (170,590 km) on the clock. The shell has quite a few rust holes, while much of the upholstery is damaged, but it's pretty obvious that this Pontiac was parked in all-original condition .
It still has the factory W72 V8 engine under the hood, and the good news here is that the drivetrain has been revived. Both the powerplant and the automatic transmission work as they should, per the seller. The vehicle is also loaded with options and has never been involved in a crash.
If it's the type of project car you've been looking for, the Can Am is available for $11,000 . For reference, examples in very good condition can fetch anywhere between $25,000 and $40,000, while concours-level cars can trade for over $50,000.

The trucking industry has fallen in love with two phrases that get tossed around in conference rooms and press releases without anyone stopping to explain them, and if you have heard the terms truck as a service and driver as a service and nodded along while quietly wondering what they actually mean for the money coming out of your account every month, you are not alone, because at a recent candid session with Daimler Truck and Daimler Truck Financial Services leadership, these concepts got pulled apart in a way that finally makes them concrete for a working carrier.
Both ideas come down to the same underlying shift. For as long as most of us have been in this business, buying a truck meant buying a truck, then arranging financing as a separate step, then paying for maintenance, insurance, and everything else out of your own pocket as those bills came due. The model now being pushed by the manufacturers flips that. Instead of a truck plus a stack of separate costs, you get a service, a single arrangement that folds many of those costs into one predictable payment. Understanding how that works, and where the catch is, matters whether you run one truck or a hundred.
What Truck As A Service Actually Is
Strip away the buzzword and truck as a service is bundling. It is the manufacturer taking the pieces you used to buy and manage separately, financing or leasing, scheduled maintenance, repair contracts, insurance, telematics, extended warranty, and the eventual resale or residual value of the equipment, and wrapping them together into one monthly rate.
Stephan Unger, who chairs Daimler Truck Financial Services, framed the company’s own evolution exactly this way, describing a shift from being a pure financing company into an integrated solutions company. The logic he laid out is that customers increasingly want ease of doing business. The fewer separate vendors, invoices, and decisions a carrier has to juggle, the more time it can spend actually moving freight, and bringing all of those services together into a single rate is the advantage the manufacturer is selling.
The most complete version of this is full-service leasing and rental, where you are not really buying the truck at all, you are paying to have a working truck available. Unger pointed to a Daimler unit in Europe called Charterway that runs more than 6,000 trucks for customers on short-term and long-term rental, with the pitch being that the customer concentrates on moving goods while the provider takes care of the machine and everything around it. The selling point that lands hardest is uptime. In that model, if a truck goes down, the provider hands you a replacement from the rental fleet so you can keep your commitments to your own customers. In North America, Daimler delivers that kind of full-service leasing through partnerships with Penske and Ryder rather than running the fleet itself, while the rest of the bundle comes through the manufacturer side.
Daimler is not a small player making a small bet here. The financial services arm operates in 21 countries with more than 30 billion euros in assets under management and leans on an A credit rating, so when the manufacturer talks about bundling the whole lifecycle of a truck, it has the balance sheet to back the offer.
What Driver As A Service Means
Driver as a service is the newer and stranger of the two, and it exists because of autonomous trucks. When the driver is no longer a person in the seat but a software system guiding the truck, the question becomes how you pay for that software, and the answer taking shape is a subscription.
Daimler described a model where the revenue streams are deliberately separated. You buy or finance the truck and the chassis the way you always have, and then the virtual driver, the autonomous system that actually does the driving, comes as a per-mile software-as-a-service charge layered on top. In other words, the truck is a capital purchase and the driving is a running subscription billed by the mile.
The company’s autonomous program centers on a redundant Freightliner Cascadia paired with a virtual driver from its subsidiary Torc Robotics, and leadership said it expects to get the driver out on a first route by the end of this year, building toward commercialization at scale around 2028. For financing, Daimler said it is prepared to structure around whatever shape that autonomous model ultimately takes. The point for carriers is that driver as a service is not a far-off abstraction. It is a payment model being designed right now, and it splits the cost of a truck into owning the metal and renting the capability.
The Ownership Question Nobody Wants To Answer
Here is where it gets philosophical, and where a reporter in the room cut straight to the heart of it by asking, if all these services are bundled into the financial contract, what does a customer actually own, and do they even have an interest in owning?
The honest answer from Daimler’s leaders was that it depends on what you choose, and that flexibility is the whole point. Unger described a menu of states, from straightforward financing where you own the truck, to leasing, to arrangements more common in Europe, with service elements added into the contract according to what the customer prefers. Kevin Bangston, who leads the financial services arm in North America as president and CEO of Daimler Truck Financial Services USA LLC, was clear that a fleet can still decide what suits it best. You can own the equipment and make monthly installments over three years, then sell and remarket it yourself. You can take an operating lease with its own financial advantages and run it for a period. Or you can layer the full ecosystem on top in whatever combination serves your cash flow and flexibility.
Importantly, Bangston said North America has not seen a fundamental shift out of ownership and into leasing, no dramatic change in the mix at this moment, just more interest in the bundling concept. So the picture is not that ownership is dying. It is that the options around it are widening, and the manufacturer is increasingly happy to sell you access to a working truck rather than only the truck itself.
One force quietly pushing carriers toward these models is residual-value uncertainty, especially with battery-electric trucks. Nobody is fully sure what a used electric truck will be worth in a few years because the battery is the big unknown. Unger noted that Daimler is willing to take on that residual risk because its battery management systems and the data it collects give it a read on the health of the truck and its battery that an individual owner does not have. When the resale value is murky, letting the manufacturer carry that risk through a lease or bundle starts to look more attractive, which is exactly why these as-a-service models tend to grow fastest around new and uncertain technology.
The Real Trade-Off For A Small Carrier
None of this is free, and the trade is straightforward once you see it. Bundling buys predictability. One monthly rate that covers the truck, the maintenance, the insurance, and the warranty means fewer surprises, and when cash flow is tight, an unexpected major repair that would otherwise sink a month becomes someone else’s problem to absorb. For an operation running thin, that certainty has real value.
What you give up is the upside of ownership. When you own the truck outright and maintain it well, you capture the resale value yourself, you build equity, and a paid-off truck becomes a margin machine. Hand the lifecycle to a provider and you trade that equity and that upside for convenience and predictability. Neither choice is automatically right. The answer depends on your breakeven, your cash position, and how much you value a steady number over a shot at the upside. The one mistake is signing into a bundle because it sounds modern without running it against what owning would actually cost and return over the same years.
Why It Matters
The move from owning trucks to subscribing to them is not a marketing trend, it is a restructuring of how capital, risk, and cost sit on a fleet’s books, shifting maintenance, insurance, warranty, and residual exposure off the operator and into a single recurring rate the manufacturer controls. For any leader responsible for fleet economics, the decision is no longer just which truck to buy but how much of the lifecycle to own versus rent, and getting that balance right against total cost of ownership and residual risk, especially as electric and autonomous equipment make resale values harder to predict, is becoming one of the more consequential financial calls a fleet makes.
This article is based on a panel discussion with Daimler Truck and Daimler Truck Financial Services leadership at the DTFS North American headquarters in Charlotte, North Carolina, featuring Eva Scherer, CFO of Daimler Truck Holding AG, Stephan Unger, chairman of Daimler Truck Financial Services, and Kevin Bangston, president and CEO of Daimler Truck Financial Services USA LLC. Figures and forward-looking statements are as presented by the executives.

Squirtle Is an Offspring of One the Most Beautiful Campers out There – Born of French Camping Design
14 photos
Photo: Carapate Aventure
Over the years, there have been hundreds if not thousands of camper models that I've written about, and very few have stood out quite like the Carapate. Well, I recently encountered some of their “newer” models, and one of which is the Squirtle or Squirt, for short.
Folks, Carapate is the name of a camper but also a brand and ever since they hit the scene years ago, they stood apart from all others with a travel trailer design that took us back to a time when camping was all about stripping away everything that cities have impregnated onto our soul and invited us to take in the very essence of the natural world.
Photo: Carapate Aventure The way the body is completed was and is one of the strongpoints for the style, with a pod-like structure that includes an oversized hatch along one side in order to open up the interior to the world around and allow us to take in all the beauty right from bed. It’s a clear reason why countless readers tune in every time we shed light on the Carapate.
While the Carapate is the flagship of the brand and has stood as the one and only unit from the brand, I recently checked back in with the French brand and come to find out, there are some “new” units available, and if I may, they still tap into the spirit of Carapate and all that this brand is about. Sources mention these models as having been around since 2024; I'm not so sure how we missed them until now.
I will shed light on the other two models that accompany the Squirt (Carapuce) over the next few days, but for now, we’ll focus primarily on this camping option as it's the most affordable in the lineup, the smallest, but also, is the only one that breaks away from the Carapate design , the one that landed them on the map. Will the Squirt take them off the radar? Let’s find out.
Photo: Carapate Aventure Right from the start, we can see that for the Squirt, the whole utility trailer style has been called upon, granting us access to a large box where we find all the systems the manufacturer offers, along with storing personal belongings, and any extras you ask for, while the upper level, or the sleeping area, is granted by the presence of a roof-top tent mounted onto a rack system.
Now, that box is still crafted from the choice material of this brand: wood. While most potential camper owners would freak out about hearing that their unit is built from wood, Carapate clearly treats this material to stand up to the elements, and if anything does need replacing, it’s easy to do.
The slide-out drawers are also crafted from this timeless building block, and it’s also here that we find access to some of the features we’ll be using while living off the land. This includes our cooking and dining gear only, and if you do ask for a fridge or cooler, it’ll be mounted outside and on the trailer’s drawbar or wherever you manage to mount it.
Photo: Carapate Aventure More wood is also found in shape of five tables or “shelves,” as Carapate calls them. These shelves are to line the lower edge of the Squirt and, if I may, are a pretty neat addition to the unit, especially for hanging around and putting a beer or book down. Dishware also falls into this category.
All this wood, chassis, and running gear make up for a camper that can weigh as little as 340 kg (750 lbs), and since it peaks at 800 kg (1,764 lbs) – it's a braked-axle trailer – it leaves us with ample cargo space more than the camper weighs on its own. Speaking of cargo, most of which will be stuffed into the box via a hatch found at the rear.
What I found rather interesting and wild about this little trailer is the fact that Carapate showcases it with features like solar panels, leading me to believe that batteries are in place and unlocking off-grid use. You’ll need to bring along plenty of water.
Photo: Carapate Aventure This leaves us with just a couple more important aspects of the Squirtle, one of which is the fact that, due to the use of the rooftop tent, this camper is limited to use in the warmer months of the year. The second is the price. According to Carapate’s website, the Squirtle is starts off at no more than €10,600, or roughly $11,900.
I’m curious to find out how you feel about that price so drop your thoughts in the comment section below.
Actually, there is one other aspect we can add to the list of traits of the Squirt, and it’s that Americans should have a very difficult time making one their own. Then again, there are several brands in the US that craft similar campers, although aluminum and steel are called upon to complete them.
Luckily, if you do want to build your own wooden Squirtle-like camper, it's clearly possible; show a couple of images to a craftsman in your area and see if you folks can make it a reality.

Rare E-Body Mopar: 1970 Barracuda Gran Coupe Needs Rescue Last Week, Great Factory Options
25 photos
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante
The debut of the greenfield project third-gen Plymouth Barracuda meant not only a transition to a new platform (E-body), to accommodate the big-block 440 and 426 Hemi (particularly the latter and its ginormous cylinder heads), but also a diversification of styles for the Mopar pony car. Unlike in previous years, the revamped Barracuda came in three distinct flavors: run-of-the-mill Barracuda, high-performing ‘Cuda, and plush Gran Coupe, like this one waiting for better days in Massachusetts.
During the 1960s, Detroit automakers dramatically diversified their product portfolios, engineering vehicles tailored to virtually every conceivable buyer preference and budget. From spartan economy compacts to full-size highway cruisers and raw quarter-mile brawlers, showroom floors offered unprecedented variety.
Yet that sharp market segmentation never stopped product planners from combining seemingly opposite philosophies into single packages, creating hybrid machines that simultaneously satisfied a buyer's appetite for high-octane performance and upscale luxury.
Plymouth launched the Valiant-based Barracuda in 1964, building over 387,000 units across three generations over 11 model years through 1974. First-generation output reached some 126,000 units from 1964 until 1966, with an all-time model year peak of 64,596 in 1965.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Second-generation production totaled over 140,000 Barracudas (the best generation regarding sales), with its best season coming in at 62,534 units in 1967. The third-generation E-body debuted in 1970, and was the longest-spanning iteration of the emblematic moniker, although it was also the lousiest in terms of money-making, with just under 115,000 copies.
1970 was the best season, at 48,867 cars, and 1974 was the all-time low, with 11,734 vehicles (but please remember production halted on April 1, ten years to the day after the Plymouth pony car was introduced on the market as the first-ever pony car).
When the E-body debuted for 1970, Plymouth split the lineup into the base Barracuda, the luxury-focused Barracuda Gran Coupe, and the muscular 'Cuda. Produced solely for the 1970 and 1971 model years, the Gran Coupe totaled 10,394 units, with 9,217 domestic-market examples (the rest were exports).
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Specifically, 1970 yielded 8,183 hardtops and 596 convertibles globally, including 7,320 hardtops and 566 convertibles stateside, while 1971 added 1,615 hardtops overall, of which 1,331 were home-market deliveries.
Designed as an upscale grand tourer, the Gran Coupe featured standard leather bucket seats, an overhead warning-light consolette, carpeted lower door panels, bright wheel lip moldings, reflective lower side stripes, and an argent tail panel.
Buyers could choose from 198- and 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six money-saving, mileage-making motors, or step up to the 230-hp 318 inch V8, the 290-hp 383-cubic-inch two-barrel V8, or the 330-hp 383-cubic-inch four-barrel V8, paired with 3- and 4-speed manuals, or 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmission.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante No, unlike the twin cousin from Dodge, the Challenger (the absolute debutant of the 1970 model year), which had the right to be both luxurious and muscle-bound at the same time, courtesy of the R/T SE combination, the Gran Coupe halted at 383 cubic inches. No 440 (single-carb of triple twos), and no 426 Hemi, unfortunately.
Still, the Gran Coupe wasn’t an “also ran” or a “was there” kind of pony car. It had its appeal, but it wasn’t that hard to miss it, in the flooded environment of 1970, dense with so many options, a buyer had to have some serious steel nerves to keep track of them all.
A surviving example of this luxury-muscle formula is inspected by Steve Magnante on his eponymous YouTube channel, a Burnt Orange 1970 Plymouth Barracuda Gran Coupe hardtop. Although its location is kept private, there is one particular detail you might find attractive about it. more on that in a moment.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante The car is part of a collection in Massachusetts, but it’s not the type of curation that involves white gloves and glass preservation jars. It’s the quintessential rust belt type of discombobulation. Its what gearheads refer to as “field find.”
Beneath its flat hood sits the L-code 290-hp 383-CID two-barrel V8, an engine Plymouth mated exclusively to the A727 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic. In 1970, the Mopar division built 1,780 Barracudas with the 383-cubic-inch two-barrel V8 and TorqueFlite, comprising 945 Gran Coupe hardtops, 54 Gran Coupe convertibles, 722 base hardtops, and 59 base convertibles.
For 1971, just 381 automatic 383-2 Barracudas were built, with 161 of them being Gran Coupe hardtops (the ragtop was cancelled after just one season, and the figures mentioned above should be a fair indicator as to why that happened). Over the two-year run, Plymouth produced 1,106 hardtops and 54 convertible Gran Coupes with this powertrain.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Pricing in 1970 positioned the Gran Coupe right between the $2,764 base Barracuda coupe and the $3,164 'Cuda hardtop. A 1970 Gran Coupe hardtop carried a base price of $2,934 with the 225 Slant-Six and $3,035 with the standard 318 V8, while the convertible started at $3,160 with the six-cylinder and $3,260 with the V8. In 1971, the Gran Coupe hardtop base price stood at $3,029 with the standard issue 318 V8.
Ordering a 1970 Gran Coupe hardtop with this specific setup required modest upcharges over the $3,035 V8 base sticker. Selecting the 290-hp 383 two-barrel added $87, as cited by Steve Magnante, and mandated the 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic at $227, bringing the base powertrain total to $3,332 before adding factory air conditioning at $358, power front disc brakes, power steering, and 15-inch Rallye wheels.
Currently offered for sale by owner Bob Doty, the Massachusetts survivor wears factory Burnt Orange paint, standard chrome bumpers, and bright wheel lip moldings that were omitted on high-performance 'Cudas for tire clearance. Its original vinyl top was peeled away, though traces of the grain remain near the roof seams. Up front, the fenders retain their Gran Coupe emblems and factory reflective side stripes, a signature 1970 safety styling cue.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Decades of street use left a quirky scar on the driver-side front fender, where a previous owner drilled a hole directly through the Gran Coupe badge to mount an aftermarket theft-alarm key switch. Under the hood, the big-block motor remains intact alongside its factory air-conditioning compressor, a thermostatic torque-drive cooling fan, a heavy-duty 26-inch radiator mandated by the climate-control system, factory power steering, and power front disc brakes.
Inside, matching Burnt Orange leather upholstery covers (well, covered when new) the front bucket seats and rear bench, though cloth-and-vinyl trim was an available factory alternative. The doors display dedicated Gran Coupe emblems and a remote driver-side mirror adjuster, while the molded headliner houses the trim-exclusive overhead warning-light console.
Rather than a floor console, the car uses a column-mounted shifter for its A727 TorqueFlite automatic alongside a Rallye gauge cluster with a 120-mph speedometer.
Photo: YouTube/Steve Magnante Out back, the argent tail panel retains its Gran Coupe emblem above a single-exhaust system still holding remnants of its factory resonator. Underneath sits a sturdy 8.75-inch rear axle, likely carrying a 3.23:1 ratio, instead of the 7.25-inch unit fitted on six-cylinder cars. Although original Burnt Orange paint with factory runs survives under the trunk lid, the rotten trunk floor requires a full replacement sheet metal to restore this rare big-block Mopar classic.
Fortunately, aftermarket body panels from Auto Metal Direct make welding in a fresh trunk pan a straightforward task for any skilled fabricator looking to return this 1970 Plymouth Barracuda Gran Coupe to the road. The rare Massachusetts luxo-pony car is currently up for sale through owner Bob Doty, and prospective buyers can find his direct contact phone number revealed by Steve Magnante at the 3:41 timestamp in the video embedded down below.

How Much Is a 27,000-Mile 2025 BMW 740i Worth Today in USA?
8 photos
Photo: Instagram | limitedspec
If you are thinking about buying a used BMW 7 Series from the new generation, then you may want to keep reading, because this example is for sale.
Hey, we said the latest generation, but that does not mean the facelift, which is only six months old. You see, the company debuted it earlier this year, and it managed to evade the Neue Klasse exterior design, just like the upcoming X7. Its front fascia looks like an evolution of its predecessor, it has a modified back end, and an entirely new interior that hasn’t escaped the Neue Klasse trend, as we are certain you already know.
You can check out the latest iteration of the BMW 7 Series, or LCI (Life Cycle Impulse) in the company’s slang, here if you want to know more about it. However, you may want to click that link after you keep reading about the pictured example, because this story is dedicated to it. You are looking at a 2025 model year car, as mentioned in the title, and it is in the 740i configuration, the vendor, @limitedpsec on Instagram, reveals.
This means that it features a 3.0-liter engine under the hood with forced induction. The gasoline burner produces 381 horsepower (386 ps/284 kW) between 5,200 and 6,250 rpm, and 384 pound-feet (520 Nm) of torque from 1,850 to 5,000 rpm. The model features an integrated starter generator, and hits 62 mph (100 kph) in a very respectable 5.4 seconds. As for the top speed, it is electronically limited to 155 mph (250 kph).
Photo: Instagram | limitedspec The pictured car sports an Alpine White paint finish complemented by the usual black bits and pieces, and appears to ride on the stock wheels. That’s good news for interested parties who are not into modded examples, because from what we can tell, this BMW 7 Series hasn’t been visited by the tuning fairy. The vendor also mentions additional gizmos, including the Shadowline blackout trim.
Other features include the glass controls on the inside, power curtains at the rear, black leather upholstery, black stitching and piping, a black headliner, the usual screens, ambient lighting, large foldable armrest at the rear, and a few other bits and bobs. The used car dealer behind the ad noted that there is no rear seat entertainment system on deck here, so occupants at the back will have to look out the window and talk to themselves. You know, the old-school way.
From what we can tell, there is nothing wrong with this BMW 7 Series , as it looks very good both inside and out. We cannot see any wear on the inside, not even on the driver’s seat outer bolsters. And that is rather surprising from a new-age machine, because it is a 2025 model year, as mentioned above. On top of that, it is not exactly a brand new car either, as the odometer read around 27,000 miles (~43,500 km) at the time of cataloging, the vendor reveals on social media.
Photo: Instagram | limitedspec Are you curious how much a 740i from the 2025 model year goes for in today’s used car market on our side of the world? One will have to prepare a minimum of $54,000 for this thing if they settle for a high-mileage example that is far from being perfect, and close to $85,000 for a barely driven one. The original MSRP was almost $98,500 for the rear-wheel drive, which is the configuration of the pictured car, and the xDrive all-wheel drive model was roughly $2,000 more expensive back then.
A fair purchase value is around $65,000 in today’s market, and you will probably be surprised to learn that in this case, the selling dealer isn’t asking an arm and a leg for the BMW 7 Series in question. In fact, this car has a very reasonable asking price, as at the time of writing, it was $61,980. And that’s below the average market value, as we already told you.
What new BMW would this sum get you today in the States? Well, a brand-new BMW X3 in the 30 xDrive configuration, for one, which has an MSRP of $51,300 attached to it. Or perhaps a base 5 Series, aka the 530i Sedan, which starts from $60,500. You shouldn’t dream about a 2027 7er, because the 740 kicks off at $99,800 with rear-wheel drive, and $102,800 for the xDrive all-wheel drive flavor. And yes, we are talking about the facelifted iteration, in case you forgot.
Now, assuming you had a budget of roughly $60,000 and the desire to get something big, spacious, luxurious, and without that many miles under its belt. Would the pictured 2025 BMW 740i make it to the top of the list? I think this is a lot of car for the money, and if you want to make it yours, then you should reach out to the vendor on social media.
